Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do restaurants cook pasta so fast?
Answer: I’m not proud to know this. And I would not recommend it to my worst enemy. As a student, I worked in a London fast food place which was pretty popular among young people. The spaghetti bolognese was actually renowned. Since the question is about cooking pasta, only two words about the sauce: stretching ingredients. We boiled the pasta in the morning, drained it and conserved the pasta in buckets filled with ice water. Every time a spaghetti was ordered, one of us grabbed a portion, put a ladle of sauce and a handful of cheap cheese on top, and microwaved it for 3 minutes. Buon appetito…or not?

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Why have canned beans become more popular than cooking dry beans?
Answer: Canned beans -and legumes in general - are ready cooked while dry beans have to soak before being cooked. Price-wise canned beans are rather cheap, so it’s all about convenience. Taste-wise there ain’t much difference, apart from the fact that canned beans are way too salty. The big difference is when canned beans are seasoned. That reduces the possibilities of preparing them notably. Then again, if it’s beans in tomato sauce you’re after, a can is an almost logical solution.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can sardines be safely consumed directly from the tin?
Answer: Yes, they come cooked and seasoned. Some people actually like them in a sandwich. With some cucumber and tomato.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Are Italian pizzas overrated?
Answer: I wouldn’t fly over to Italy just for pizza, but once you’re here, they’re worth trying. There are over one hundred and eighty thousand pizzerias in Italy, so some will be better than others. There are some simple rules that may avoid you being disappointed

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some ways to add flavor to risotto without using butter or cheese?
Answer: Most fish, and seafood in general, risottos don’t feature cheese nor butter. I personally use a very neutral rather than olive oil (grape seed). The creaminess is obtained by stirring the rice through the cooking process while the taste comes from the fish broth -fumet.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Why do Italians eat pasta every day?
Answer: In Italy nobody eats just pasta, it is but the carrier for the condiment. In a very similar way other cultures have rice, potatoes or bread every day. Say you have zucchini, you then prepare them with pasta. It is quick, tasty and healthy. The quantity of pasta served averagely doesn’t exceed 100 grams per person. Furthermore, ever since health pundits have been preaching against carbohydrates, many Italians have been renouncing to daily pasta. And though I am not Italian by birth, a day without pasta ain’t complete for me.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Sardines are really healthy. Now they don't taste very good. How long will it take for sardines to taste good?
Answer: Your initial reaction may very well be finding sardines unpleasant in taste; this phenomenon often occurs when presented with new food. Sometimes it takes a while to get used to a new taste, a process known as acquiring taste. Now your question is a tricky one: it combines health as well as taste. Making sardines taste ‘good’ is rather easy but usually it reduces the healthy factor. Frying your sardines for example will make them pretty irresistible, almost addictive. After removing the guts, head and spine, the sardines bathe in salted water first and vinegar afterwards. They are then deep fried. Tasty, yes, healthy…not really. When you chop up sardine filets and mix them with breadcrumb, raisins, pine nuts, grated cheese and some mint, the result will be a tad healthier but with a more distinct sardine taste. When sardine filets are marinated in lemon juice and serve them with a little garlic, well then you are getting all the health benefits. It is basically like popping omega three pills.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How can I use the world's best olive oil to enhance my cooking?
Answer: Don’t consider it oil but rather an ointment. Good olive oil should be used to crown a dish, and a crown is put on at the very end. A simple tomato salad topped off with a drizzle of olive oil will make your guest frantically mop up the juice with some bread. A little olive oil on fresh boiled pasta does miracles, too. Anyway, use your best olive oil ‘raw’, don’t heat it as it will lose much of its fragrancy.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you suggest some delicious Italian dishes that include onions as an ingredient?
Answer: What about sweet sour tuna fish, Sicilian style. After frying your tuna steaks and setting them apart, fry onion, just a little more than you think you need, add sugar and vinegar. Underneath that sweet sour onion lay the steaks, and yes, it is often topped off with a little mint.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the recipe for making Italian bread for bruschetta?
Answer: Making bruschette is a way to use old bread which is then toasted or roasted. No use baking fresh bread to let it get stale. and classically topped of with diced tomato and a drizzle of olive oil There is no actual recipe, so it is up to you. You can make them as fancy as you please. With slice of bottarga - cured fish roe - for example. In Italy bruschette are served as starters or to accompany an aperitif. .

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How can traditional Italian desserts like cannoli and tiramisu be made healthier without using eggs?
Answer: Whereas tiramusù contains eggs, cannoli don’t. And then again, there are plenty of tiramisù recipes without eggs. Sweetened ricotta in a fried crust ain’t exactly healthy. But that’s hardly the point here. Why on earth do you worry about health when preparing desserts? Have yourself a piece of fruit.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How many types of Parmigiano cheese are there in Italy?
Answer: There is only on Parmigiano Reggiano. The difference come with the seasoning: the longer that process takes, the more intense -and expensive- the cheese gets. The use too changes, as it would be a crying shame to grate a 60 months old Parmigiano on your pasta. Being very dense it is even impossible to cut in in slices, so break it into pieces. Parmigiano Reggiano is, together with olive oil, the most counterfeited product. The rule of thumb is that you pay what you get. There are no cheap versions.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is it common for real parmesan cheese to have holes in it?
Answer: Parmigano cheese does not have holes, it is very compact. And it is actually projected not to have any holes, so if you find a cheese labelled parmigiano with holes, leave it there.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What inspired you to start cooking from scratch instead of using pre-made meals?
Answer: What inspired me cooking from scratch were, actually, pre-made meals. Those meals crossed my path a long time ago, and for just a moment they seemed a convenient solution. A couple of minutes in a microwave and you had a pretty decent meal. What a mirage. Indeed, when eaten alone, on your desk, it saves you time (then again, you are not eating but rather getting nutritional intake). Though once you prepare them for more than two people, it becomes unsettling. The first tray will be cold when the third tray is ready. That is what triggered us -students sharing a house- to start cooking. Sometimes together, sometimes alternating, sometimes cheating. Not only did we save money, we learned that preparing a pretty decent meal could be fun, healthy and a challenged us to become better.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the cheapest food that is more delicious in the world?
Answer: Foraging is free, fun and not half as dangerous as some news outlets like to depict it. Even when it comes to mushrooms. Sure you need some basic knowledge. Don’t go haphazardly picking mushrooms, let some expert do it first and learn. Initially show your expert what your found and after not too long you’ll be able to pick the right ones. In Sicily, after rain not only sunshine but also little snails come. They are known a babbaluci. Together with the petrichor -the earthy smell after rain- these little snails make your day. They are then prepared with garlic and parsley. A feast. And what about wild aspargus!? They grow well hidden but once you know where to look, picking them becomes almost addictive. Most countries have their fair share of things to forage, and it’s always a nice way to pass some quality time.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What's the most unique or exotic kitchen gadget you've used in your cooking?
Answer: For many years I had a ‘presse-canard’ in my kitchen. Not this shiny thing, but that’s for later. Just for the record, a presse canard is used to crush duck bones in order to obtain the juice and use it in a so-called brown sauce. Such a bone juicer doesn’t do anything else and is hence not all that often used. Added to the fact that these contraptions are terribly expensive, they don’t feature all that frequently in kitchens, not even in the professional ones. There was no way I could afford a presse canard as a student so I asked my grandfather to help me build one. He was a carpenter with little knowledge of smithery but eagerly accepted the challenge and we ended up with was aesthetically probably not great, but a perfectly working presse canard. My presse canard gained a lot of value when I decided to bring it to Italy, a couple of years after I settled there. The thing weighed about 40 pounds, way more than what the airline company allowed. Anyway, the presse canard featured on a shelf for years and I was always happy when someone asked me what-the-hell it was. Till the shelf collapsed. Repairing the crater in the wooden floor cost me quite a bit and the machine was broken. When I moved to the place were I now live, the presse canard was issue of heated discussions and it eventually ended up in one of the boxes we brought to the trash park. But on a shelf I put the framed picture of my grandfather. And I am always happy when asked who the man in the picture is.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do I incorporate garlic into my cooking?
Answer: There is a golden rule regarding the use of garlic in cooking: the finer it is chopped, the more intense the taste. In the Italian cuisine for example those extremes find their way in green pesto on one hand and ‘garlic in its shirt’ on the other. In the first example raw garlic is crushed and will give you that pungent yet pleasant taste. Inversely, many Italian recipes only want a hint of garlic. Unpeeled cloves are fried in olive oil and then removed.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is there a common misconception that Italians do not eat spaghetti?
Answer: Italian do eat spaghetti, actually it apparently the preferred pasta shape. What they don’t eat is ‘spaghetti sauce’ as it is known abroad where meat, tomato and too many other ingredients are combined. Their version, ragù, is simpler and eaten for special occasions as it has to cook for quite a long time. And, furthermore, ragù is usually not served with spaghetti but long, flat pasta like tagliatelle. Try to guess which is Italian and which is not…

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can I freeze pesto with nuts?
Answer: Sure you can, it is an excellent solution when preparing a big batch of pesto. Pesto doesn’t have to be the ubiquitous green one, there are a myriad of variations on the theme. A couple of things should be pointed out though. Green pesto, aka Genovese, is prepared with pine nuts. Sicilian pesto with almonds and other variations use other nuts. A personal favourite contains hazelnuts. The only fresh ingredient used in most pestos is basil. So pesto is prepared when basil grows profusely, hence large batches are prepared. You can top a jar full of pesto off with olive oil and keep it in the fridge. It will last for over a week. For longer conservation freezing is an excellent solution. Just keep in mind that pesto is not reheated, so let it thaw for a couple of hours and do not use the microwave cut corners.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is your best recipe for dried fava beans?
Answer: Dear John, that depends on how the fava beans are dried. Fresh fava beans are gently dried in the late spring sun till the outer skin becomes hard. Part of these beans will be used to plant new ones in November. You can prepare them ‘rabbit style’. Let them soak overnight and then boil them with the adding of onion, garlic and a bay leaf. Season with salt, olive oil and oregano. The name cunigghiu -rabbit refers to the way they are eaten: you hold the bean between thumb, index and middle finger, bite the top off and with the right pressure of your fingers separate the skin from the inside. As a rabbit does. Apparently. The mere fact this food is eaten with your hands makes it outstanding. And who doesn’t lick their fingers afterwards, only enjoys it partly. My favourite way is turning them into a puree, here known as macco. This is really easy to prepare and it makes me wonder why this dish is not eaten all over the world. You basically boil your beans to pulp and season it with salt, pepper and olive oil. Though I like to add some pieces of fennel in mine.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do you make the perfect garlic pasta?
Answer: As it often happens with Italian pasta dishes, it comes down to personal preferences. Each cook prepares it with a personal touch. And though there are only few ingredients, the preparations are countless. A very basic aglio olio e peperoncino looks something like this: A fast -often emergency- meal that is devoid of presumption. One could step it up notch and make it creamier using the ‘risottare’ technique where undercooked pasta is prepared as if it were risotto. Or go wild and make it a gourmet garlic pasta, though this is an oxymoron: pasta with garlic and oil is a simple dish by definition.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the reason behind people ordering pizza as their main course at Italian restaurants?
Answer: Pizza is a main course in Italy. Served in pizzerias rather than restaurants, but a main course anyway. Why? Because it is a full meal. For the very hungry clients there are starters and desserts.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is your preferred bean dish and why? Can it be made from pre-prepared beans or do you prefer to cook them from scratch?
Answer: That’s tough choice but I’d settle for a plate of macco di fave, fava bean puree. Fava beans -aka broad beans- are pretty ubiquitous here in Sicily. They are planted right after the olive harvest and serve as a cover crop. The beans ripen around March and herald spring. The first fava beans are small and tender and can be cooked as they come. Later beans need to be husked or dried. Anyway, macco is no more than overcooked beans, seasoned with salt and olive oil. And some wild fennel if available. Just for the record, dried fava beans cost next to nothing. The recipe: fry diced onion, carrot and some garlic in olive oil, add your fava beans and water and let it simmer away till you obtain a puree; top it off with a generous splash of olive oil. Serve with bread. One more thing: fava beans can be dangerous if you suffer from favism. So better check that out before diving in.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the recommended cooking time for fresh ravioli before adding it to sauce?
Answer: There is an easy, infallible method for cooking fresh ravioli; add your ravioli to slightly salted boiling water and wait till they come afloat. Depending on the size this may take two to four minutes. Just make sure they don’t boil any longer as they will open. And add them straight to the sauce to avoid sticking.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do you rate Yusuf Dikec at the 2024 Olympics?
Answer: I happened to watch the tennis match yesterday. Great game but what struck me was what happened at the award ceremony. All three had put on a watch at their left wrist, making sure it showed. Don’t get me wrong, I don’t mind these athletes taking sponsor money. Apparently most athletes do similar things, whether it’s through wearing glasses, hats or other accessories. What is striking that mister Yusuf Dikec was there just for his sport, in which he excels, somehow renouncing to sponsorships and we consider that weird.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you suggest some popular Italian summer dishes?
Answer: I am sorry for all the people who happened reading my previous answers, but I’m going for pasta with tenerumi, again. And more than an Italian summer dish, it is a Sicilian one. Tenerumi are the tender velvety leaves and sprouts of a local courgette. They are boiled and then set aside. You will be boiling your pasta in that same water. And for the occasion you can break spaghetti (or other long pasta) all you want. Fry garlic in olive oil, add diced (peeled) tomato. Then it’s time to assemble. Teneremi can be served with more or less liquid. It is a typical summer dish and served piping hot, which may sound insane knowing that Sicilian summers are scorching, yet it brings relief.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the reason behind Italians eating spaghetti with tomato sauce instead of other types of pasta like penne or rigatoni?
Answer: Tomato sauce, unlike other condiments, can be served with most types of pasta, not only spaghetti. Though I can’t give you a good reason other than being ubiquitous, it tastes better with spaghetti anyway.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you list some of the oldest Italian desserts?
Answer: One of the oldest, tastiest and most interesting desserts must be biancomangiare. It is believed the dish come to life when Arab and Norman culture overlapped during the reign of Frederic II (around 1200) in Palermo. Originally milk was thickened with starch and flavoured with almonds though in the following years there was a savoury offspring, using chicken. Being delicious the dish spread through the whole of Europe and can now be found in most countries. The sweet version that is. As you asked for a list, here’s another classic. Sorbetto Again, a recipe with Arab roots. This proto ice cream is made with a mix of fruit juice, water and sugar.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Why are Italian grandmothers known for their cooking skills? What happened to the other talented Italian cooks?
Answer: Practice makes perfect. Preparing two -or more- meals ago for years flattens out initial mistakes; this goes for cooking grandmothers all over the world, not just the Italian ones. Alas, cooking every day often was not a choice but pure necessity, a task more than and expression of gastronomic enthusiasm. With some luck a granddaughter, a daughter in law or other female presence come to help. Luck for the grandmother and the people helping her, because that’s how they learned to cook. Until not too long ago, home cooking was a female affair in Italy. With the deepest respect possible, most grandmothers are excellent cooks but not chefs. Grannies cooking is appreciated because it is unsurprising, traditional if you please.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What dishes do you cook for your picky eaters?
Answer: Over here there are some standard dishes made to please picky eaters -and children. No eggs, no butter; cutlets are first passed in olive oil and then breaded with a mix of breadcrumbs and grated cheese. An evergreen that seems to please ever the fussiest eaters. Ring shaped pasta with fried aubergine, boiled eggs, peas and ragù.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is it common for Italians to make their own spaghetti sauce from scratch or do they typically buy jarred sauces like everyone else?
Answer: So it’s Italians against everyone else now? I am pretty sure that some of the ‘everyone else’ prepares ragù or spaghetti sauce at home and that some Italians indeed buy ready made ragù in jars. The simple fact they feature in Italian supermarkets means there is a market for them. Anyway, making ragù is an act of love. It takes a while to prepare it properly and people it is served to appreciate that fact. It should be said that ragù -in Italy- is prepared for special occasions, not on a daily basis.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do you make a creamy risotto?
Answer: The term creamy may be confusing here, as it refers to an aspect rather than the presence of actual cream. The creaminess of risotto is obtained due to release of starch while preparing risotto, and that is the reason specific -starchy- rice is used. Extra creaminess comes from the last step in the risotto preparation, when the heat is switched off and butter and grated cheese is added. This process is known as mantecare in Italian. By no means add cream to your risotto as it will flatten out the taste of your concoction.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the most expensive dish ever created, and what ingredients are used?
Answer: Preparing expensive food to show off wealth is something humans have been doing for a long time. And the biggest battle was that between Mark Antony and Cleopatra, about two thousand years ago. Mark Antony was known for his lavish dinners. In order to impress his lover, the Egyptian queen Cleopatra. He had the finest ingredients from all corners of the Roman empire brought in and served the most amazing dishes nobody had ever seen, let alone eaten before. Cleopatra was only mildly impressed and assured she’d do better, way better. Hosting Mark Antony she slipped off one of her pearl earrings, crushed it and let is (probably only partly) in a goblet of wine. Now, them earring were the biggest in existence and just one of them was worth 1764 pound of gold (800kg) or in modern money somewhere around 45 million dollars. Recipe: Crush an enormous pearl and let it sit for about 10 minutes acidic wine.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Why are mushrooms commonly used in dishes like risotto and pasta, even though they may not add much flavor? Why not just eat them on their own if that is their main purpose?
Answer: First of all, pardon my presuming. You refer to the Italian cuisine, I guess, as you mention risotto and pasta. And secondly, mushrooms being a general name, I presume we’re talking about the king of mushrooms, porcini. Now they are indeed often used used in pasta and risotto dishes. I strongly disagree about them not having much flavour, but that is of course a personal matter. You can have your mushrooms on their own indeed. It’s pretty easy. Clean your porcini and slice them. Fry a clove of garlic in olive oil, then add your mushroom and a pinch of salt. Then it is the dry-wet-dry process: your mushroom will give of moisture that will slowly evaporate. Some fresh chopped parsley on top and you have yourself a winner. This is usually served as a side dish. As the porcini season is rather short, you can dry them. Slice them and let them hanging in a ventilated place till they are thoroughly dry. They will last till the next mushroom season. It is amazing how they come back to life -as a matter of speaking- when immersed in lukewarm water. That same water will be mushroom flavoured, so don’t throw it away. You can use these dried porcini for pasta and risotto recipes, alas not for the recipe above.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is risotto considered as important as pasta in Italian cuisine? Can you share a good recipe for risotto?
Answer: More than a matter of importance, it is a matter of frequency. Risotto is a great way to prepare rice but surely less eaten, considered the whole of Italy. In the North, especially in rice-growing regions that may be different, but again, overall speaking… When well executed all risotto recipes are great. It is of utter importance to use the right rice, risotto rice: Carnaroli, Roma, Sant'Andrea, Vialone nano, Arborio. They are starchy and cook in about twenty minutes. Instead of water, broth is used, vegetables, meat or fish. Most risottos, after having added your broth bit by bit and having stirred regularly, are finished with butter and cheese. The last action with the heat off. After toasting the rice, add white wine and broth a little later. Half way through add your previously stir fried porcini mushrooms. Once your rice is al dente - with a little bite to it - switch of the heat, add butter and grated parmigiano cheese.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How can one express gratitude to a chef after trying their dishes?
Answer: Tell the waiter, tell your friends, come back for another meal, just don’t insist to see the chef him or herself after your meal. These people, you see, are at work, managing the kitchen, and though they’d be flattered by your praising, there is no time for them to interrupt their activity. The opposite is also true, when you wish to complain about your food. Tell your waiter what’s wrong and he or she will be the bringer of bad news to the kitchen. Restaurants where the chef roams the table are suspicious, imho.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do I make a dip with pesto?
Answer: Pesto as such is way to strong to be used as a dip, it needs to be diluted. If you want to play it hardcore, mix fresh pesto with mayonnaise, preferably home made. A little lighter when mixed with Greek yogurt, don’t forget to add a pinch of salt.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How is pasta shaped?
Answer: You can either shape it manually or use a moulding device. The first requires quite some dexterity especially replicating the same shape over and over again. This requires exercise and perseverance but once mastered, the result is marvellous. Shapes vary all over Italy. The picture features busiati, typical for western Sicily. Hand shaped pasta is usually short pasta. The classic Italian moulding device allows you to stretch out the dough and then cut in large strands. Lastly there are machines available that press dough through a mould, allowing various shapes

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: If each region of Italy has their own sauce for pasta. What are your favorite sauces the Italians use for pasta?
Answer: Each region uses ready available ingredients, which are quite different from region to region. And though it may seem these ‘sauces’ or condiments are the result from recipes written in stone, they slightly evolve over time, adapting to the modern palate. To illustrate, in Sicily we do not only have fresh sardines, pine nuts and raisins, locals gather wild fennel in winter. That combination results in pasta with sardines. There are as many variations as people preparing this, which makes it only more exiting. The same goes for other regions, so it’s hard to settle for one favourite dish. Apart from regional dishes, there are the Italian dishes, probably originating from one specific region but then spread all over the country. Tomato sauce, pesto, even carbonara. With such a variety of pasta dishes, picking one is a punishment, not a choice.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How would you describe a good Italian food restaurant menu? Are there any other popular dishes in Italy besides pizza and pasta?
Answer: This depends on the restaurant and your budget. When hitting a trattoria, the menu should list the so-called classics. Very unsurprising in offer and taste, so exactly what you are after when eating there. When going to a restaurant one may expect something a tad more sophisticated, local ingredients, a touch of class. Regarding the offer apart from pasta and pizza: pizza is best eaten in a pizzeria, not in any other kind of restaurant. Most, if not all, restaurants offer pasta. It comes as ‘primi’. You could go for rise or simply skip it and go for secondi, meat or fish.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Why do people add excess water when cooking spaghetti? Is there a specific reason or is it just a tradition?
Answer: There are two main reasons for using a lot of water when boiling spaghetti, and pasta in general. First of all, it allows people who do not have the experience in preparing pasta to avoid a sticky mess. The second reason is related; when using abundant water, much of the starch is drained. This results in a ‘lighter’ spaghetti.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do I cook pasta with cheese?
Answer: There are quite some ingredients where cheese is the main ingredient in Italian pasta recipes. Pasta with cheeses, four of them. Usually made with gorgonzola, emmental, fontina and provolone. Not the lightest of the pasta dishes and therefore often prepared in winter time and in the mountains. The cheeses are cut small and slightly melted in a pan, often with a dash of cream - once you go heavy, go all the way. Add your fresh boiled pasta and stir. A classic Italian -Roman- dish. Start with putting your pasta to a boil; this is important as you need the starchy water to continue.Roast crushed black pepper in a pan and when it starts to smell peppery, add a ladle of the water your pasta is boiling it. Add some water grated pecorino cheese (pecorino Romano) and stir till obtaining a smooth mixture. Add the pasta to the pan followed by the cheese mix. Stir as if there were no tomorrow. More than the cheese it will be the starchy water giving that velvety aspect. Ok, ok, ricotta is technically speaking not cheese, but anyway. So easy, so tasty it has to be mentioned. Add a ladle of the water your pasta boils in to a bowl of ricotta. Add that to your fresh boiled pasta. Some black pepper and you’re ready. Personally I like a dash of tomato sauce with it.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some foods that do not taste good when deep fried with batter?
Answer: I’m not a fan of fried ice cream The crust is insignificant and doesn’t add to your ice cream. Even the apparent contraction doesn’t convince. There are so many nice ways to serve ice cream, and battering and frying it is not one of them.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is salt typically added when making stock or broth from scratch?
Answer: You should never do that as it jeopardises the outcome. Broth -and stock- boils for a very long time and much of the water evaporates. What tastes fine at the beginning will become useful at the end. It is recommended to add salt when your broth is done. And even then, a tiny amount of salt is enough, especially when you’ll be using it for sauces. The culprit in the salty stock story are the ready-made versions you find in the shop. They are indeed handy and somehow tasty but have little or nothing to do with the home made version. Just for the record: preparing beef stock is time consuming, but you can make a large batch and freeze it. Making stock is also very satisfying and the perfume…

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the recommended cooking time for spaghetti? What is the preferred method for cooking it?
Answer: It depends on the brand but all feature the average cooking time on the package. It further depends how you like your spaghetti, or pasta in general. A couple of days ago my friend Ciccio prepared a marvellous spaghetti with clams, but as he likes his spaghetti undercooked, I had some trouble fully enjoying them. The same goes with the pasta my ex mother in law prepares, but the other way round: as she long has dental issues, she slightly overcooks hers. Both Ciccio and my mother in law would have issues with my just al dente preference. So it goes. As for the cooking method: bring a pot with water to a boil, add salt and your spaghetti. Give them an occasional stir - this avoids sticking and further releases starch needed to get a creamy result.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you explain the difference between Turkish pide and pizza?
Answer: One of the main differences is the absence of yeast in Turkish pide. The seasoning on the Turkish pide is freer, with less people making making a fuzz about what should be on it. And then there is the form; pide is rugby ball shaped, a pizza football shaped. (Football/soccer ball) The presence of yeast in pizza has often been discussed. Just to be clear, no yeast, no pizza. The question is how long pizza should rise and what yeast to use. Some say that excessive yeast -or a too short rising period - causes health problems. Till not so long ago it was not unusual to be thirsty at night after eating pizza. As yeast dies at 38 degrees C (100F) and pizza is baked in a 350 C (660F) hot oven, this is unlikely to have any truth in it. What could be true is that your body will have more trouble digesting. More likely to cause that nocturnal thirst are the salty ingredients often added on pizza. Nowadays pizza making has stepped up with pizzaioli using starter dough, new (old) kinds of flour and more selected toppings (rather than just opening a can). Masters at work; pide and pizza

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the general opinion of Italians towards Americanized versions of their cuisine, such as spaghetti and meatballs and pizza?
Answer: The American-Italian cuisine is an intrinsic part of the Italian cuisine, made and conceived by people with Italian roots. It sure is different from what the homeland prepares but nevertheless Italian food. If you migrate, you don’t lose your origins, you add to them. People complaining about this are shortsighted especially because they don’t actually (have to) eat the American variations. I like the idea to add a suffix to the dishes concocted in the USA, all’americana. As we do in Italy referring to various regions. There are more serious things to get upset over than innovation.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some methods to prevent pasta from sticking together before boiling?
Answer: Don’t add oil, don’t rinse. It’s pretty easy. Use abundant water and give your pasta an occasional stir while it boils. Once done, drain add your pasta to a sauce or season it immediately. If you let it sit for over a minute, it will get as sticky as a child holding a popsicle. This batch is for your least favourite dog.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some nutritious ingredients that can be added to vegetable soup?
Answer: Not so long ago vegetable soup was daily served in many parts of the Western world, boiling down available vegetables, in the best case scenario accompanied by a piece of bread. With some luck there were dried legumes to be added and increase the nutritional value. What’s for sure that there was no recipe and the lack of meat was due to not having any, not out of ethical considerations. Sometimes, with some luck and in special occasions, meat was added, not the fancy parts though. As it boiled for quite some time, even the toughest parts soften down. Nowadays it is not that unusual to find meat in vegetable soup though some utter that this is an oxymoron. For them: a vegetable-based soup can have meat in it to increase the nutritious value. As in this wonderful Columbian sanchocho.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Does fried fish belong with spaghetti?
Answer: Not really. Have your fried fish after the spaghetti, in the same plate if washing up is what you lead to that idea. Fried fish should be crunchy, and loses that characteristic when added to pasta. Ideally fried fish is served on and absorbing surface, so the excessive drains.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is it common to eat spaghetti with fish?
Answer: Pasta with fish -and meat for that matter- are not all that common in Italy. Those dishes are served for special occasions. And when pasta and fish are combined, it is usually not with spaghetti as it is difficult to eat. Better use short and thicker pasta in order it all mixes together. The exception on rule are clams; they should come with spaghetti

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you share your thoughts on the Italian dish lasagna?
Answer: There is only on thing better than fresh baked lasagne. I’ll leave it for last. In Italy lasagne are served for festivities, prepared by an expert on the subject. The dish doesn’t come as ‘lasagne’ but as mom’s lasagne, zia Caterina’s lasagne etc. A dish you look forward to eat. The prepared quantities are enormous and since other food follows, some has to remain. Reheated in that same tray it will get crunchy and imho even better than the fresh one. The fact you’ll be scrubbing that tray is so worth it. Italian top chef Massimo Buttura made it one of his signature plates.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can canned garbanzo beans be used as a substitute for cooked garbanzo beans in hummus? Will it affect the consistency of the hummus?
Answer: Canned garbanzo beans are cooked garbanzo beans, so it’s short cut. The only difference is the high sodium content in canned beans. Better rinse them before turning them into hummus. Consistency-wise there is no notable difference with home-boiled beans. And though I know many purists will preach against the use of canned beans, they are a valid alternative, especially when you live in a country where garbanzo beans are imported anyway.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is it necessary to cover spaghetti while boiling it?
Answer: Though it is not wrong and in no-way influences the outcome of your spaghetti, Italians do not cover the pot with boiling spaghetti. They’d give the spaghetti an occasional stir and towards the end of the boiling process fish out a strand to check the done-ness. What is necessary is abundant water and salt.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Do you cook after work?
Answer: I might do some prep work before going to work, but the actual cooking is done in the evening, after work. On a typical day that would be around eight o’clock and in the best case scenario we all participate. Someone prepares the salad, someone sets the table, someone does the actual cooking. It is precious to be together, especially after a long day. I confess that when being alone, little time goes into cooking. We have pasta for lunch and therefore meat or fish -or eggs, legumes, cheese - in the evening. Nothing special, nothing too time consuming. Yesterday we had a hamburger…

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Why is pasta called penne?
Answer: Not all pasta is called penne, only penne are. The Italian names often refer to the shape of pasta. Farfalle because they resemble butterflies, spaghetti because they look like strings. Penne take their name because they look like old-time pens. Penne is written with two n’s. If not you get this

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How is Italian pasta different from American pasta?
Answer: The way pasta is conceived, and hence prepared, seems to be different. In Italy pasta is usually very simple, straightforward and comes in portions of about 100g (3.5oz). It hardly ever contains proteins and even rarer cream. This is enough to carry on in Italy, but could be complemented with a secondo, a meat or fish dish. As in America -and in other countries- pasta is a main dish, they tend to add, to enrich. This American pasta dish could be decomposed into three Italian dishes, if the curly parsley would be substituted with the flat one. Anyway, this is a difference, not a judgement.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the recipe for Italian mashed potatoes?
Answer: Can you see any difference with non-Italian mashed potatoes? No? Well, these have some freshly grated parmigiano cheese in them. Is it any good? Is it worth it? Frankly? Imho, there is no need as it doesn’t make the puré any better but my Italian friends swear by adding it.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do I make a healthy Italian vegetable recipe?
Answer: Last Saturday for lunch when the temperature exceeded 35 degrees, 95F, we had a piping hot pasta with tenerumi. I can’t think of a healthier dish as it not only contains veggies, it somehow mitigates the heat outside. Wash and boil your zucchini leaves for about twenty minutes, then remove the leaves and cut them Don’t drain the water, set it aside. Fry a clove of garlic in a pan with olive oil and then add cut up cherry tomatoes. They should hiss when thrown in. Boil the pasta in the water your zucchini leaves have boiled in, add the tomato and you’re done. I like mine a little less watery and with salted ricotta.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some effective methods to enhance the flavor of a basic tomato sauce for pasta?
Answer: Start by frying a clove of garlic in olive oil, then add your sauce. Remove the garlic and let it get dense, to a tar-like consistency. Less water means more taste and the sticky sauce coats your pasta perfectly You could add some dried tomatoes (umami bombs). In that case, pass your sauce through a vegetable mill to avoid chunks. The result should something like this:

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are two dishes using different offals?
Answer: I’ll start off with one and when you tried it, another one may follow. Pane ca meusa, a spleen sandwich is an emblematic dishes in the city of Palermo. Apart from spleen it contains lung and trachea, all veal. After being boiled it is fried in lard. Hence the specially designed slightly tilted pot; once ordered the chef slides some of the meat toward the lower part with the melted lard. No italics nor inverted comes with the word chef; people preparing this delicacy are true artists, hence chefs. You will then have to chose whether to have it simple, schietta, with lemon juice and salt or ‘married’, maritata, topped off with grated cheese. In some places they serve it with fresh ricotta. Schiettta maritata

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you suggest any recipes that use dry caviar (not sturgeon) as an ingredient?
Answer: I am not really sure what you refer to, but it could be dried roe in general, so the answer concerns that. Dried fish roe can be added, grated, to many dishes. A personal favourite is pasta with bottarga, mullet roe. Really easy to prepare as it is pasta with garlic and oil topped off with a generous grating of bottarga. Finely sliced on a bruschetta (dried tuna roe here) is magnificent though quite overwhelming. Allow me this advice: never buy your dried fish roe ready grated; it is low quality and almost tasteless. Grate when needed. As it comes with a certain cost, it is nice to grate it to served pasta or food, much alike when grating truffle

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are the reasons for the variety of ingredients and recipes in the French dish Ratatouille?
Answer: Most Mediterranean countries have dishes similar to ratatouille, for a good reason. There is this part of the summer season when lots of vegetables ripen together. French ratatouille is an excellent solution for this abundance. Very similar is Greek briam, Spanish pisto, Italian peperonata and even caponata. The variety of recipes is due to the availability of the ingredients. And to vogue, as for example the nice looking version is ubiquitous

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are the advantages of using milk instead of water when boiling pasta?
Answer: There is not one single advantage; it is a bad idea, full stop. Technical issues Taste

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is it safe to add raw chickpeas to soups without cooking them first, similar to lentils or beans?
Answer: It is far from safe if you don’t want to boil that soup for an hour. Raw chickpeas are hard as stone and you could actually ruin somebody’s teeth. So if you’re not a dentist desperate for patients, avoid.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you substitute flour for bread crumbs when making chicken tenders?
Answer: Sure, but you will end up with a different texture, a different dish. When using flour, fry your chicken in some oil and than add liquid. White wine, marsala, lemon juice, you name it. The flour will help to bind the sauce.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Where did pepperoni originate from and why is it not considered a traditional Italian dish?
Answer: Pepperoni is a schoolbook example of syncretism, when two or more ideas overlap and amalgamate in something new. It is said, and the name pepperoni sustains that, this particular cured meat has Italian roots, in salame piccante. Pork meat is mixed with chili peppers and salt (sometimes also black pepper and fennel seeds) and dried. Italian immigrants mixed pork and beef - which was widely available- with paprika and other spices. The paprika idea probably come from Eastern European immigrants. Other ingredients where then once ready available in the USA. Pepperoni is not considered a typical Italian cured meat because it was invented in the States and uses different ingredients than their Italian counterpart. Which does not mean it isn’t delicious. Just not Italian.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Have you ever met a person who later became famous?
Answer: I am not absolutely sure, but like to believe so. Somewhere in the nineties, traveling in South America, I met this jolly English chap. Meeting foreigners was normal as they -we- stayed in pretty run down hostels most of the time, saving money for more exiting things than sleeping. Anyway, this guy was witty and practical, and he even spoke some decent Spanish. We hung out for a couple of days, not doing anything special. Only when stumbling on a documentary on Vice, I remembered him. Now, if you are DEA or MI6 or similar, don’t come knocking on my door as apart from a fond recollection, I’ve got nothing to tell. Then again, I’m not even sure it was him.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do cooking techniques differ between fresh and dried pastas?
Answer: Cooking fresh pasta is a tad more demanding as there is no estimated cooking time. You’ll have to try for yourself to see when it’s cooked. It averagely takes less time to boil fresh pasta, which easily turns in an unattractive mash. Anyway, both fresh and dried pasta is added to slightly salted boiling water. Easy peasy.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: I don't understand why some people salt their pasta water only after it comes to a boil? Is there a good reason for this? What is the reason for it chemically?
Answer: It’s more of a habit than a reasonable procedure. Sure, this way you avoid to salt your water twice, and apparently adding salt to cold water, before boiling, ruins your pots. The idea that salted water boils later has been debunked, unless you use loads of salt.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some common breakfast options at restaurants in your town or city?
Answer: There aren’t any restaurants offering this serve but most, if not all, bars in Palermo have fresh cornetti and nothing says Italian breakfast louder than cornetti. They are similar yet different from a croissant - cornetti have egg in the dough. They can be empty or filled with cream, custard, pistachio, chocolate, jam, ricotta, mixed berries and so on. Most people have them standing at the bar, with a cappuccino, café latte or just coffee. Just for the record, cornetti are typical breakfast food as well as the favourite snack for partying night owls.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the reason for putting sauce on top of pasta instead of mixing it beforehand?
Answer: I think you can write it down to a combination of laziness and culinary ignorance. The ‘mixing it beforehand’ is a fundamental step in preparing pasta. Fresh boiled pasta goes in the pan with the sauce or condiment, together with some of the water your pasta boiled in. And a drizzle of olive oil. When you thoroughly mix the result will be creamy pasta. And all your pasta will be coated equally. If you ladle sauce on pasta, not only you’ll have to mix it yourself and probably stain your clothes, the pasta will cool down and get sticky.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is snapping spaghetti illegal in Italy?
Answer: Oh dear, here we go again. Breaking spaghetti has nothing to do with illegality but rather with logics. Spaghetti is chosen because of its form, for the pleasure of turning it around your fork in them. Any shorter strands make the eating more difficult as they fall off the form. Also true that any longer spaghetti would result in overloaded forks. That’s why artisanal spaghetti is snapped at the bow (the bow is the result of the rod spaghetti dries on) In some occasions spaghetti is broken in small pieces, when used in soup like pastas, as here with unmatched tenerumi. These are eaten with a spoon.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the proper way to eat caviar from a can or jar?
Answer: It is very fancy to serve a can of caviar on ice. Guests then spoon a little caviar over pieces of bread. Lots of ink has flown over what spoon you should use when serving caviar, and apparently all spoons but silver ones are fine. The fish roe may oxidate when it comes in contact with silver, and change taste. Now, caviar is expensive, so serving it with a plastic spoon seems an oxymoron. Mother of pearl, horn, tortoise shell present themselves way better. And how cool is it to have a caviar spoon laying around. Certainly not the way to eat caviar The winner of a caviar eating contest shoved 5,000 dollars worth down his throat. And he surely doesn’t seem happy.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How would you describe the taste of spaghetti with olive oil and Parmesan cheese?
Answer: Unsurprising, familiar, hearty. The adding of fresh ground black pepper is a welcome optional.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is prosciutto not a topping option on Pizza Hut pizzas in Italy?
Answer: There are no Pizza Huts in Italy. And the few Domino’s closed down. There are some chain pizzeria places - Crazy pizza for example- but they aren’t all that popular. On the other hand there are about 183 thousand pizzerias in Italy, covering all budgets, taste and vicinity.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the proper way to express gratitude for a meal after dinner?
Answer: That really depends on where you find yourself dining. Here in Sicily for example people express gratitude by leaving some food on their plate. It shows you ate to satisfaction, that you’re full, so there was enough food and the host did a good job. Ad empty plate on the other hand shows you were hungry and maybe you still are, and might offend the host. The same mechanism occurs when people refuse to take the last item on a tray during a dinner.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are the reasons for people buying canned baked beans instead of making their own?
Answer: Preparing your own beans -in tomato sauce I presume you’re asking - is quite demanding, time-wise anyway. Soaking the dried beans overnight, cooking them for a considerable time, preparing the sauce… Cracking open a can, with that familiar taste, is easy and immediate. And as canned beans are inexpensive, the choice is obvious.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What do you do when you´ve eaten a lot more than usual?
Answer: Sicilian festivities are heavily food-based. Those are days where lunch lasts till dinner, and as skipping dinner is considered insane, you end up with a sore tummy. That’s when the canarino, the little canary, comes in. Don’t worry, no birds are sacrificed. The name refers to the yellow colour. Bring water to a boil, add two bayleaves and the peel of half a lemon. Let it boil for about ten minutes, and when cooled down your medicine is ready. Pretty effective indeed. Another local digestive drink comes as autista, the driver, as it was first prepared for a taxi driver who over-ate (so the story goes). Anyway, here baking soda is added to a mix of water and lemon juice. It will start foaming immediately -acid and baking soda do that, remember your chemistry lesson. Drink the glass, bottom up.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How can cauliflower and potatoes be cooked together without becoming mushy? What are some recommended cooking methods?
Answer: As they have quite different cooking times, one could add the cauliflower to already boiling potatoes; that is frankly pretty complicated and seldom results in an acceptable result. You could use one of those pots with separate baskets, something Italians use when they want to boil two different kinds of pasta at the same time. Mind you, this is an interesting technique as you save energy.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some ways to make a delicious lasagna without putting in too much effort?
Answer: This a school example of a contradiction in terms. Making lasagne is demanding, laborious, frankly, a toil. But also an act of pure love. Preparing and serving lasagne to family or friends is nothing less than a long, warm hug, a culinary way of saying I love you. Every shortcut subtracts, and scars the final result. Till you end up with something like this:

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How can I make an inexpensive cut of beef taste amazing without using any special ingredients or cooking methods?
Answer: Some dishes ask for inexpensive cuts, and as it happens, their preparation is simple and ingredients few. Right up your alley. This is ideal meat to prepare a spezzatino, Italian beef stew. It usually features carrots, celery and potatoes. Seasoned with thyme, salt pepper and a generous splash of red wine, it is simmered till the meat is tender. A pressure cooker reduces the cooking time notably while the result is pretty similar. Just for the record, the bits sticking to the bottom of your pot can be used to season a plate of pasta, known in Sicily as pasta alla glassa (or grassa) Another nice way is to boil your meat. These odd looking chunks will turn in a delicious dish when boiled together with onion, carrots and celery. Add some black pepper, cloves and bay leaves. Both recipes would be tasteless when prepared with expensive and lean cuts.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is a recipe for serving raw fish at home? Can you make tartar sauce without using mayonnaise and egg?
Answer: Goodness gracious! Tartar sauce is fine when served with deep fried fish. As it is battered and or breaded, some sauce helps to give it freshness. But that same sauce nullifies the taste of raw fish. If you are going to prepare, serve or eat raw fish, you want it to taste as such, no? You can add a drizzle of olive oil, fresh herbs, some salt and lemon if you please. Or nothing at all. I’d leave out the mint as well in this shrimp tartare, though it looks good. When preparing fish tartare, make sure to freeze your fresh fish for at least four days, in order to eliminate potential parasites.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is there a recommended time to stop adding condiments to food?
Answer: Often less is more, or better, more is worse. But when exactly to stop is hard to tell, as it shows when foreigners have a take on the Italian cuisine. Some may state this is enriching food though the word overkill is more appropriate. A Sicilian cannolo, with sweetened ricotta, chocolate chips and candied orange peel becomes this when you don’t know how to say STOP Or a nice parmigiana, eggplant, tomato sauce and cheese becomes this behemoth

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is your opinion on mayonnaise mixed with ketchup?
Answer: In Italy this is known as salsa rosa, pink sauce. It comes with chips, sandwiches and a seventies classic, Cocktail di gamberi, prawn in pink sauce, rigorously served in a glass. Sure, it’s childish, overpowering in taste and not all that healthy, but what the heck, sometimes you have to let out the child in you.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How much do you usually pay for an espresso or cappuccino at a cafe bar in Italy?
Answer: I had a very similar question just a couple of days ago by a visting English friend. While she was gathering her stuff from the table I went to pay at the counter. As I never have cappuccino or coffee sitting outside a bar, I was quite shocked to pay six euros fifty. Scrutinising the receipt my friend asked me how much I paid. ‘Six euros for a cappuccino? That’s London prices!’ she exclaimed. The matter of fact, a cappuccino was two euros, a coffee one twenty and the ‘cornetto’ (a cream filled croissant kind of pastry) one eighty. An other whopping one euro because we had our little breakfast outside. Very kindly she promised the next breakfast was on her.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Do you have a favorite cooking oil besides olive oil?
Answer: Grape seed oil, by far. First of all because it is a byproduct of wine making; having wine and oil is a win-win. After wine, oil, the remains are used a biomass, saving resources notably. This oil is furthermore very light in taste and has a pretty high smoking point. So whether you use it to prepare mayonnaise or fry in, you’re in good company.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Do Italians have meals with most or all courses brought to table at once? Once antipasti is served, do cooks typically leave the table to prepare pasta, then again to do meat, veg, salad, then back for dessert, coffee, etc.? Is banquet-style a thing?
Answer: On an average weekday an Italian meal, at least here in the south, consists in either pasta or proteins, usually divided between lunch and dinner. The salad may be brought to the table along but will often be eaten apart anyway. Festivities are different. Apart being extremely food-focused and these lunches take hours, the cook will indeed disappear to the kitchen after each course. Truth be told, many of the dishes are prepared ahead of time and only need some reheating. Most people take offence when you even suggest there is no need to change plates between courses. The banquet-style, in my experience, is asking for trouble. Being hungry -these lunches tend to start late- people throw themselves on the antipasti as there were no tomorrow and then eating little or nothing of what is yet to come.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are the differences in flavor and quality between light and regular olive oil?
Answer: Just to be sure there was no such a thing as light olive oil, I googled the term and almost fell off my chair. Apparently light olive oil is regular olive oil from which taste and colour is distracted. Why on earth such a crime is committed, I have no idea. I can’t get my head around this; if you don’t like olive oil, buy other, neutral oil. Avoid these petty shenanigans.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the modern-day version of Roman spaghetti alla Carbonara in Italy? What are the ingredients and how is it traditionally prepared?
Answer: Just last week we had a carbonara di zucchini in Rome. It is prepared pretty much as you would prepare classic carbonara but instead of guanciale, you use fried zucchini. Was it any good? Frankly I don’t care all that much for carbonara in general and the vegetarian version did not change my opinion. Just for the record, carbonara may not be as popular as regular carbonara, but it was on the menu of a typical Roman restaurant, and plenty of locals were having it.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What was your biggest culture shock going to Europe?
Answer: Though I have lived most my life in dear old Europe, the shock it had ready was pretty tough. For over a year I worked in Southern Africa, between Zambia, Malawi and Zimbabwe, crossing borders almost weekly. It took little time to understand that a small gift to the custom officers smoothened the passage notably. A senior colleague explained that a neatly folded twenty dollar note in your passport assured a superficial luggage search while a fifty one guaranteed a warm welcome and a cooled soft drink. Not great, probably deplorable, but indeed effective. After every trip, you just added a new banknote. Not really sure about this but I seem to remember we wrote these gifts of as travel costs to our agency. Anyway, flying back to Europe I forgot about the twenty dollar note sitting in my passport. The French custom officer fished it out as if it were a full diaper and asked me to step aside. As he would not listen to our explanation, my travel companion called out another custom officer, one with African roots, asking him to explain his colleague that what I did was normal in Africa. Deeply offended he scolded my travel companion but let him off since he had no money in his passport. Just before stepping away he shouted: ‘You should have put a fifty, Ian’. That little joke further upset the custom officers and I ended up paying a thousand dollar fine, losing my train to London and the happiness to be back in Europe.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some ways to make pasta and broccoli taste good?
Answer: An easy and interesting way is to boil -without overdoing it- your florets and then transfer them in a pan with olive oil and garlic. Boil your pasta in the same water so it gets that extra flavour. Once boiled, add your pasta to the broccoli and stir, adding a cup of the water your pasta and broccoli boiled in. No need for any other ingredients, except maybe a light dusting of parmigiano cheese.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you suggest some delicious recipes for cooking red mullet (fish)?
Answer: One of the simplest ways to prepare small red mullet is to fry them; open the belly and remove the guts, pass them in flour and fry away A tad more demanding but still pretty easy is preparing them alla Livornese (triglie all’acqua pazza). Fry some garlic in a pan, add parsley and later peeled tomatoes. When the sauce gets denser, add your gutted mullet and let them simmer for about ten minutes.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can I use frozen cooked shrimps in recipes?
Answer: Dear Ali, whereas frozen fresh shrimp has a happy afterlife, cooked shrimp has little or nothing to add to dishes. You can use it to give some consistency or texture to dishes, but taste-wise it won’t do any good. When the shrimp is already part of a dish and then frozen, it will have given some of it taste to the other ingredients and a hint can be recognised. My two cents is to use just the right amount of fresh shrimp when preparing and freeze the rest.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do I cook broccolli and make it taste good?
Answer: Broccoli are not indispensable in our diet; if you don’t like how they taste, don’t prepare and serve them. No need for boiling the living daylight out of them, covering them with heavy sauces or hiding them.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What type of sauce is typically used in Sicilian pizza?
Answer: There ain’t such a thing as a Sicilian pizza. Very popular and similar if you please is the sfincione. The dough is thick and spongy, the sauce is made with onion (lots of them) tomato sauce and anchovy. This is then topped off with breadcrumb, cheese, oregano and more anchovy. Not for the weak stomachs. Another quite typical Sicilian take on pizza is the rianata,(Western part of Sicily) Rianata translates as oregano, and that is what that pizza is all about. The tomato sauce is enriched with onion, garlic, pecorino cheese and anchovy. Generously dusted with dried oregano. Though this comes in the ‘classic’ round pizza form, the try-baked version is more common

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the most effective way to reheat leftover pizza: on the stove or in the microwave?
Answer: As restoring leftover pizza to its original state is impossible, why not eating it cold? Breakfast of champions! Microwaving makes it soggy, heating it in pan dry.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the most popular type of pizza in Italy? Is it different from the pizza commonly found in other countries?
Answer: According to different delivery sites, the margherita pizza is -and remains- the most popular one. Very straightforward, with a topping of tomato sauce and mozzarella, it brings you back to the essence, something Italians seems to appreciate more than an overload of ingredients. Abroad there is a tendency that the more ingredients -and the tastier they are- the better the pizza becomes.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is potato a popular food in Italy?
Answer: Growing potatoes in Sicily isn’t all that evident as much of the soil is rocky which is far from ideal. The potatoes remain small and harvesting is usually a manual affair for the machines often break down hitting rocks. Yet potatoes are quite popular, not as staple food but rather as an interesting vegetable. There is a beautiful expression that says that who eats potatoes, never dies, Cu mancia patati un mori mai. Potatoes are used with pasta With meat (lamb here) Savoury pies or in salads (insalata vastasa)

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the best recipe made by potatoes in your country or home?
Answer: The best dish featuring potatoes in my adopted home country, Italy, must be pasta with potatoes. Different regions have different preparations. I like this one: fry chopped onion on olive oil, add diced potatoes and some water later. Cover and let it simmer away; halfway through, add some saffron. Mix your fresh boiled pasta with the mixture and serve piping hot. This dish brings instant happiness. And for those worrying about carbs on carbs, get a life.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How much oregano should you add to pasta sauce?
Answer: Dear Lynnette, in Italy oregano is hardly ever added to tomato sauce as this is a very powerful herb that tends to overwhelm rather than add flavour. There are exceptions, but it is then clearly stated oregano has been added. As in rianata, the Sicilian for oregano. Generally, avoid adding it and if you really like it, add a light dusting right at the end of the cooking process. Oregano gets really bitter when cooked.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Italians, is it wrong to eat pasta on the same plate as another dish (eg. a beef dish or a fish dish)? If so, why? Isn't it more practical to just eat everything together, instead of keeping them separate?
Answer: In Italy pasta comes before meat or fish, and yes, when home you might use the same plate. Specially if you’re a student, home alone or plain lazy. Still, in this case you’ll eat the two dishes separately, no chance of seeing this around The reason? They are two different dishes, supposed to be savoured one at the time.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the reason for the high prices of Italian restaurants in Italy compared to other countries?
Answer: Well first of all, Italian restaurants in Italy are just restaurants. Only when serving other than Italian food, they will advertise so. Now, when Italians go to a restaurant, they want something more than what they could prepare and eat a home, often fancier and harder to prepare dishes. Preferably something that restaurant specialises in, like particular fish or meat dishes. Hence you pay that little more. If Italians don’t want to pay too much and still want to eat out, they have quite some options, from tavola calda, to trattorie. These establishments serve unsurprising, homely food. And charge very reasonably. Abroad this distinction is not made, so what restaurants may serve would be nothing more than trattoria or tavola calda food.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: I like to try new pasta shapes. I bought Fusilloni which are giant (more than double the size of) Fusilli. Are there any recipes associated with this pasta?
Answer: Dear Joseph, I must admit new and unusual kinds of pasta attract me, too. Truth be told, those impulsive purchased packs often end up in the pantry till some day we run out of conventional pasta and have no choice but to prepare it. Here is my two cents. Fusilloni are indeed big and hence very pastacy, and therefore difficult to serve with chunky sauce or condiments as it wouldn’t fit your mouth. And since they are big, you need a strong sauce or condiment, one that sticks so every bite is fully seasoned. Pesto is a nice option. My preference goes to red or Trapanese pesto. Crush garlic, peeled almonds, basil, pecorino cheese peeled tomato and add olive oil. This pesto is then add and thoroughly mixed with your fresh boiled fusilloni.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do you make homemade pasta from scratch?
Answer: Homemade pasta is a rarity, even in Italy; it’s fancy yet the effort is usually more appreciated than the eventual result. It requires quite some skill and sets you back quite some time leaving you with a messed up kitchen. With excellent dried pasta ready available, making fresh pasta tends to be an act of overachieving. Anyway, there are two main ways to make fresh pasta; with or without eggs. Eggless pasta needs water to prepare the dough. And that little salt to make it more elastic. The exception, still a rarity, is when making filled pasta like tortellini, ravioli etc. The stuff supermarkets sell is usually of dismal quality. And as you just have to roll the fresh pasta dough out before filling it, this is pretty easy.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What sets an Italian salad apart from a regular salad?
Answer: In the recent past more than now, a green salad was just a bowl of lettuce, to be seasoned with the oil and vinegar that came along with such an order. Still today Italian salads are usually vegetable based and served apart. If you please to have a regular salad, go for insalata mista. Which will still be underseasoned to the non Italian palate.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is liver and onions a popular dish? What are some ways to prepare it to make it taste good?
Answer: Please allow me a short Monday-morning rant. The popularity of offal meat is definitely in decline; ever since supermarkets took over the task as house hold meat delivering station from local butchers, brain, liver, kidneys, heart and tongue have become rare. All supermarkets seem to sell are hardly recognisable cuts that need the icon of the animal in order to know what it is. This tendency may derive from the attempt to conceal the fact that meat comes from actual animals. Offal meat clearly states this connection to the animal and is hence less popular than anonymous slices packed in styrofoam and covered with cling film. Anyway, the most popular Italian dish using liver must be fegato alla Veneziana, Venetian style liver. It is a wonderful dish that should be tried. Fry sliced onion and a bay leave in olive oil. Do this over a low fire as the onion should soften without browning. Clean and cut the liver in strips and add them to the onion. A generous glass of white wine, season with salt and let it bubble away for no more than five minutes. Switch off the heat and add cold butter, stir and serve.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What can you add to lentils to make them more appealing to people who don't like lentils?
Answer: Leftover lentils can be turned into polpette Pass half of the lentils through a vegetable mill, add grated cheese, an egg, breadcrumbs and seasoning to your pleasure. Fry and serve piping hot. When we prepare lentil soup some is set apart, as it would finish once it reaches the table As you can see, the soup is already seasoned, so no need to adjust it. Depending on how liquid the soup is, add more breadcrumbs. You can do this with most lentil dishes; dhal for example makes excellent polpette

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the difference between Italian herbs and regular herbs or spices?
Answer: The main herbs used in the Italian cuisine are basil, parsley, rosemary and origano. The first two fresh, the other dried. Sage can be used dried as well as fresh. Anyway, they are never added all at once. Hence avoid this abhorrence when you want to prepare Italian food I’m not sure what you mean with regular herbs and spices.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is a simple way to prepare young green asparagus without sacrificing its taste or flavor? How can we incorporate it into a dish with rice or pasta?
Answer: Fresh asparagus are ideal for risotto as well as pasta. Clean the asparagus -set aside the hard parts- and steam them briefly. Cut them in rings and set the tips aside. Fry an onion in olive oil and add your rice. Half a glass of white wine and then broth is added. Pop the unusable part of the asparagus in there as well as the liquid you obtained when steaming. Half way through - after about eight minutes- add the asparagus. When your rice is cooked, switch off the heat and add butter and grated parmigiano cheese. Only then add the tips. Steam your asparagus, cut the tips and blend the stalks with some olive oil, grated cheese and water your pasta boiled in. Personally I don’t mind popping in some hazelnuts. Add your pasta to this paste, stir thoroughly and then add the tips.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How do you make a real Italian spaghetti sauce, and how long do you have to cook it?
Answer: Dear Margaret, rather than pernicketiness, see this as an elucidation; what abroad comes as spaghetti sauce is known as ragù alla Bolognese. And more than spaghetti, it is served with tagliatelle or fettuccine. Probably a tad over the top, but this recipe was deposited by the Italian Academy of Cuisine at the Chamber of Commerce in 1982. The recipe calls for a mix of coarsely ground beef and pork, pancetta, carrot, celery, onion, tomato puree and paste, milk and white wine. As you would do with a stew, brown your pancetta and then add the diced vegetables. (though this step is often inverted) Next the beef goes in. Take your time browning it, then add wine and once the alcohol has evaporated add the milk and little later the tomato puree and paste. Let this simmer away for at least two hours. Season toward the end. Truth be told Margaret, every family has its own way of preparing this dish, but at the end of the day, it’s always with these ingredients. Rather than adding ingredients, they are left out, which sets it apart from the foreign versions. Ragù is a festive dish, mainly because of the long cooking time.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the reason behind adding water to pasta sauce to enhance its taste?
Answer: There are two reasons for doing so. With the adding of liquid you deglazes a hot pan, and all the yummy parts sticking to the bottom come off and enrich your sauce. The second reason is to obtain a creamier result. Being rich in starch the liquid will help you to thicken the sauce. See if you can spot the difference… vs

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the reason for Italy not having a national dish like other countries? Are there any dishes that are commonly associated with all or most regions in Italy?
Answer: A national dish, eaten and appreciated in the whole of Italy, might be pasta with tomato sauce. Even though that is pretty vague, as people tend to season and prepare their sauces as they know it, calling it the proper way. Pasta al sugo pleases most palates in Italy.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Can you suggest a suitable name for an Italian restaurant that specializes in pizza and pasta?
Answer: Cities, regions, even rivers and lakes do the trick. Make sure to use the Italian names, making that choice more plausible. Don’t overplay your cards, people will suppose and sometimes pretend your cuisine is somehow linked to the name of the restaurant. If you name your joint say Firenze, make sure to serve steaks, if you name it Napoli, serving polenta dishes would be awkward. When using a name, make sure to put a da in front of it; it means at. Da Mario means At Mario’s place. Which has a homely touch to it. Surnames don’t need the da. Avoid surnames that are hard to pronounce in your country. Names like Schillaci or Magnotta are usually mispronounced abroad, and if that is your real name, each time you answer the phone, a shiver will run down your spine. Monuments, objects, famous Italians and so on. Ponte vecchio, Il colosseo, Garibaldi, la padella. Again, avoid the ones that are difficult to pronounce; la forchetta -the fork or il cucchiaio -the spoon- are indeed nice names but pronounced in English or other languages they become atrocious.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is it common in Italy not to emulsify aglio e olio pasta, or is such a recipe original?
Answer: oh dear, pasta with garlic and oil is a quick emergency recipe conceived to still urgent hunger. Usually it looks something like this, and satisfies most eaters: You could indeed, without even spending much more time, obtain this: There ain’t no real recipe for garlic and oil pasta; one thing it is not supposed to be is a fancy dish.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Why do many recipes for classic Italian dishes contain errors, such as incorrect cooking times and ingredient amounts? Is this due to attempts to make the recipes more sophisticated, or is there another reason behind it?
Answer: I’ve written quite some recipes, so consider this a self defence rather than an answer. Sure, they are similar and some state that a recipe is a real-life example of an algorithm. Or you can see it as the difference between a crock pot and on stove cooking. A crock pot keeps the exact temperature and can be programmed to obtain the requested result. When you cook on a stove, this is impossible as gas -or whatever your energy source is- is hard to control to the degree. Even the pot or pan you use can make a significant difference. It deals with pretty much the same issue. Until a certain degree one can weigh ingredients and indicate cooking time. But no one in his right mind is going to state how much, say, two artichokes weigh; stating it’s two artichokes seems enough. Some things simple depend on personal taste and there the writer of the recipe weighs in -pardon the pun. The Italian term QB is quite saying: quanto basta, as needed. It drive the pedant to the wall but is very truthful at the end. When writing a recipe you’re not actually cooking that recipe, you are sitting behind a keyboard, using notes and trying to make it as straightforward as possible. Some things will slip your mind, things you take for granted. You may embellish some things, simplify others

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What's your favorite recipe for spring pasta?
Answer: Every spring, there is a short period in which the three main ingredients can be found fresh: peas, artichokes and fava beans. Combing them you get what in Sicily it is known as frittella. This can be eaten as such or served with pasta. Fortunately these ingredients are easily frozen and hence the dish can be eaten all year round, but nothing in the world beats the fresh version. Once you have the ingredients, it’s all pretty straightforward: fry on onion, add lightly boiled (quartered) artichokes, fava beans and peas. And if you want to be a hero, add some fresh wild fennel.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What type of Italian cheese is best for melting in a grilled sandwich?
Answer: Apart from the fact your cheese has to actually melt, it is all very personal. All you need is your favourite cheese that has at least a 40% water content. A personal favourite is piacentinu Ennese, a sheep milk cheese produced in the heart of Sicily. The colour is the result of the adding of saffron, which is grown in that area. It also contains black pepper corns.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is organic olive oil better for cooking?
Answer: Better use your organic -and hence expensive- oil for seasoning dishes rather than cooking. You can add it to most savoury dishes, from fish to meat, from pasta to salads. To complete the answer, yes, organic oil is indeed the better choice. You could use run-off-the-mill oil for the actual cooking and top the dish off with some really good oil.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How many kgs are on 3 liters of olive oil?
Answer: That would be around 2.7 kilos. A litre of olive oil weighs about 920 grams (a little less than water, something you may have noticed as oil floats on water). The reason olive oil is often expressed in weight rather than in volume is because at the mill the oil is weighted and the price is based on the weight.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What type of mozzarella is recommended for making pizza at home: fresh or shredded?
Answer: There are two kinds of mozzarella for preparing pizza. The dry and shredded mozzarella, mainly used for pizza and fresh mozzarella The first kind is used as base on which other ingredients can be added.
