Question: What are some creative recipes or uses for watermelon beyond just slicing and eating it?
Answer: A personal favourite. Remove the pips and juice a watermelon. For every litre of juice add about ninety grams of sugar. Add a stick of cinnamon. Heat the liquid. Pour some of the liquid in a cup and mix with ninety grams of cornstarch and add it back to the hot liquid. Switch off the heat as it starts boiling, remove the cinnamon and pour the liquid in a mould-moulds. Once set you can top it off with chocolate and or pistachio. Diced watermelon, feta cheese, fresh mint, a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of salt. Summer on a plate. Thick slices on the barbecue; an excellent way to end the day. Probably not the most common risotto but not half as bad as it looks. Use a stronger cheese than parmesan; seasoned pecorino for example.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Does adding salt to the water affect the taste or texture of boiled spaghetti noodles?
Answer: Much ink has been spilled over this issue, especially on how much and when salt should be added to the water. Harold McGee, an authority on gastronomic science says that: ‘Salt in the cooking water not only flavours the noodles, but limits starch gelation and so reduces cooking losses and stickiness’. Not adding salt to pasta -out of health reasons- is usually the last step before giving up altogether on pasta. Unsalted pasta is bland, even when mixed with sauce.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Have you ever tried eating or drinking something because you saw it mentioned in a work of fiction (book or movie)? And how did you like it?
Answer: Tanqueray and tonic, my favorite drink, the Ramones sang in ‘Somebody put something in my drink’. A message a teenager could not ignore. I wouldn’t consider it anymore but back then it was pure gold.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Is it effective to add olive oil to pasta water? If yes, what is the recommended amount to use?
Answer: Adding olive oil to pasta water is a no-no. First of all because olive oil is expensive and by adding it to the water your pasta boils in is a pure and utter waste. It’s an old wives’ tale that adding oil to pasta water prevents it from sticking together. It will furthermore coat your pasta which prevents it from soaking up sauce. Once you boiled your pasta, drained it and added it to your sauce, you can pour in olive oil, preferably when the heat it off. This results in a creamy pasta dish.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How did pineapple become a popular ingredient in Italian cuisine despite it not being a traditional Italian food?
Answer: Pineapple is pretty popular as desert fruit in Italy and it usually comes as a ‘little boat’ or barchetta or in a macedonia, a fruit salad It is though not used in savoury dishes. The idea that Italians only eat traditional Italian food is laughable; they eat what they like, no matter whether rooted in Italian culture or not.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some possible reasons for people being bad at cooking and not improving over time, even when cooking for themselves?
Answer: Not everybody loves or even enjoys cooking. Which doesn’t mean they don’t like to eat well. My ex wife was one of these and that wasn’t, by far, her worst defect. And she once forgot to fry the eggplant to make parmigiano, her favourite dish. She even told me what all the fuss what about as she prepared the dish in minutes. Before eating them, that is. Anyway, don’t get upset with people not liking to cook. Be nice, and do it for them.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: How can I prevent pasta from becoming mushy or sticky? What is the secret to cooking perfectly al dente pasta?
Answer: It all comes down to timing. Not just the time your pasta bubbles away but also adding it immediately to your sauce. If you please to have your pasta al dente, boil it for little under the recommended time given on the package as it will continue to cook in your sauce. In order to have dry pasta, add a little of the water it boiled in. Keep on practising.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: If we were to guess your region based on a culinary specialty, what would that food be?
Answer: Cannoli… No nonsense cannoli: fried tube-shaped shells filled with a mixture of ricotta and sugar. Chocolate chips if you please.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: Does cinnamon go good with pasta?
Answer: Until I actually tried it, I would have said no. Pasta with fresh ricotta and cinnamon is surprisingly good. The idea that cinnamon belongs to deserts and sweets in general is very limiting. It is surely not often found in pasta dishes, but well worth a try.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What are some Italian dishes that use breadcrumbs?
Answer: In Sicily breadcrumb is taken to the next level; it is roasted with a little olive oil and used to top off some iconic pasta dishes. Anchovy, garlic pasta with muddica atturata, toasted breadcrumbs. Pasta con le sarde, pasta with sardines, wild fennel and breadcrumb. broccoli arriminati, green cauliflower, tomato sauce, raisins and pine nuts, again with breadcrumb

Question: What is the recommended method for reheating pesto pasta?
Answer: This is quite a problem. Pesto is a cold prepared condiment that should not be heated, let alone reheated. This is one of the reasons you use mortar and pestle to prepare it instead of blender. The heat created by the blades ruins your pesto. Whereas some pasta can be reheated, preferably by frying in pan, pasta with pesto can’t. Pesto isn’t cheap, so use your maths and don’t serve more pasta than needed. A rule of thumb, in Italy, 50 grams (1,7oz) is needed for 85 grams (3oz) of pasta. Savour rather than stuff.

Question: What is the cost comparison between homemade pesto and store-bought pesto? Is it more cost-effective to make your own pesto or buy it from the store and make pasta at home?
Answer: On average store-bought pesto costs less. Depending where you live, the ingredients for pesto Genovese can set you back quite a bit. Good olive oil doesn’t come cheap, and neither do pine nuts. Alas, using cheap -or worse, substitute - ingredients is not an option. Industrial pesto makers cut corners in order to supply supermarkets with a low-priced product. Check the ingredients on the back when purchasing. Good pesto is not cheap; if money is an issue, better cook something else.

Question: What are some reasons why people may not like pineapple on pizza? Is it purely a matter of personal preference?
Answer: Pineapple on pizza is probably the most polarised culinary topic, especially regarding the Italian cuisine. Liking or disliking this concoction has little to do with actual taste but rather with taking position. Truth be told, many Italians loathe the idea of having this tropical fruit on their pizza, and the mere idea makes them shiver, though very few of them actually tried it. One reason for the aversion lays probably in the fact that pineapple is usually served cold, as a desert. Finding it on a pizza seems wrong. Another reason is that pine apple pizza did not originate in Italy and therefore considered aberrant. The sweet salt issue by itself is not an issue. Maybe not the most popular pizza but accepted as good anyway is the pizza with pears, nuts and gorgonzola.

Question: What are some ways to make ground pork taste like sausage?
Answer: In order to make Sicilian sausage you’ll need rather fatty pork meat, about 3/10. It is then mixed with salt, black pepper and fennel seeds. You can add some white wine. After a night sitting well covered in the fridge, you have your sausage meat.

Question: How can breaded eggplant be made without using flour or eggs?
Answer: You can use just oil and breadcrumb to prepare your eggplant. Eggplant are spongy and absorb oil easily, so in order to avoid a greasy result, brush them with oil rather than soak them in it. Season your breadcrumb with grated cheese, oregano and even some finely chopped garlic if you please. You can either fry them in oil -better use vegetable oil- or oven bake them.

Question: How does one prevent garlic odour after eating?
Answer: Parsley is the perfect antidote to the garlic odour. And that is why you often see them together in Italian recipes. Parsley mitigates the odour but then it tends to stick between your teeth…

Question: What are some common ways that Italians cook eggplants at home?
Answer: In Sicily caponata is a pretty common dish, and I wonder why it never made it as a popular dish abroad. Fried eggplant, onion, celery, olives, capers and tomato sauce are seasoned with a little sugar and vinegar. An excellent starter or just eaten with a piece of bread.

Question: What is your go-to appetizer at Italian restaurants and what do you enjoy about it?
Answer: When going to a restaurant that serves fish, a platter of of raw fish is hard to resist. Some Mazara prawn, a langoustine and some tuna tartare. Only trustworthy places offer raw fish, as it doesn’t come without risks. When the fish is not fresh, the joy is short-lived. Putting it on the menu is a sign of confidence and quality. What really matters is that good restaurants have excellent fish suppliers offering stuff that we mortals have no access to.

Question: What are some alternatives to pine nuts in pesto sauce? Are pine nuts necessary for the authentic flavor of pesto sauce?
Answer: When preparing Pesto alla Genovese, there is no alternative. The nuts have to be pine nuts to recreate the dish. And not just pine nuts, you need Mediterranean pine nuts. Not out of some highbrow whim, but they do taste different. The Mediterranean ones have this particular resin taste while the Chinese tend to have a bitter aftertaste and the Pakistani nuts are oilier. Mediterranean pine nut cost double or even more. For other kinds of pesto you can use the nuts of your choice. In Italy those are usually almonds or walnuts.

Question: What is the primary ingredient in traditional Italian pesto?
Answer: Quantity-wise that would be basil, olive oil and cheese. But it would be nothing without pine nuts, garlic and oil. And you should use a mortar and pestle to prepare it, not a blender. Not out of nostalgic reasons but that is the only way you can see how your pesto is coming forth. You have full control and will end up with the perfect pesto, every time. Whacking everything a blender may be faster -is faster- but with an uncertain outcome.

Question: Can you suggest a recipe for using leftover steamed cauliflower?
Answer: Here are two recipes, a starter and a pasta dish. Is that ok for you? Polpette di cavolfiore Lightly mash your cauliflower with a fork, add breadcrumb, cheese (pecorino or parmigiano) and and egg. Roll little balls and fry them. Pasta con i broccoli arriminiati, Sicilian style cauliflower A quite elaborated dish but so worth the effort and though ideally made with boiled cauliflower (as you need some of the water it boiled in and pasta should be cooked in that some water), steamed cauliflower will do the trick. Fry diced onion in pan, add some anchovy fillets. Let the anchovy reduce in a pulp and then add pine nuts, raisins and your cauliflower. I like to add some tomato paste but that is just an option. Add some water and stir regularly -arriminato is the Sicilian for stirred. This pasta dish doesn’t come with cheese but rather with toasted breadcrumb.

Question: Can olive oil be used as a substitute for butter in a traditional risotto recipe? How would the results differ?
Answer: You can, or maybe should, start with olive oil when frying your onion and toasting your rice. The finishing touch, what Italians call mantecare is usually done with butter. Mantecare comes from the Spanish word for butter, manteca-mantequilla. As much as I adore olive oil, and even though the result is creamy when using it, butter is better So, you can but shouldn’t.

Question: What is the reason behind Italians using tomato sauce instead of just adding tomatoes to pasta?
Answer: The reason is called seasonability; there are plenty of tomatoes in summer and little or none in winter. Turning tomatoes into sauce is a good way to conserve them. Whereas in the past many made their own sauce, today Italians mainly buy their sauce in the supermarket. And there are some rather good tomato sauces on the market, usually more expensive than run-of-the-mill ones.

Question: How can I remove excess water from cooked spaghetti without sacrificing its flavor?

Question: What is the very popular dish we cook using a lot of milk?

Question: What is the traditional way of eating spaghetti alla puttanesca in Sicily? Is it typically served with any side dishes or is it eaten as a main meal?

Question: Are there any authentic Italian restaurants outside of Italy? How can one identify them and where can they be found?
Answer: It should be emphasised that restaurant in Italy don’t serve home cuisine. The reason people go to a restaurant is to have something slightly different of what they eat every day. If they please to have home cuisine, they go to a trattoria, places specialised in unsurprising, highly recognisable dishes. These joints often look like this: An Italian restaurant, even when serving Italian food, will put more effort in their menus and arrangements. They have an extensive wine list and a more daring menu. One could state they are more formal. All too often, when abroad, the two somehow mix. Anyway, a good, ‘authentic’ if you like that term, restaurant will offer food that is usually not common in your country. As Italians migrated all over the world, Italian restaurant are ubiquitous. The best way, or better, the only way to know what they are worth, is going there and eat.

Question: What is the easiest way to boil noodles or pasta?
Answer: Surely for pasta and presumably also for noodles, the old fashion way works best. Bring your water to a boil, add salt and your pasta. This way you have a clear idea on the cooking time and don’t risk ending up with a mush. Pasta as well as noodles are boiled when needed. As soon as they are taken from the boiling water, they are seasoned or added to sauce. That way they won’t stick.
